figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Motivation. (a) Conventional pipelines rely on image resizing or local cropping, which inevitably discard either fine-grained generated artifacts or content. (b) In contrast, we process the image at its original resolution and represent it as multiple bags of instances across multiple scales, thereby preserving both global context and fine-grained details. (c) During inference, image-level predictions are obtained via falsification-driven aggregation of instance-level scores, where a single decisive instance is sufficient to classify the image as fake. A three-panel diagram contrasts conventional image-level detection with the proposed falsification-driven strategies. Panel a starts from a baseball photograph containing players and a bird. Resizing removes fine details, while a local crop removes contextual content; both altered inputs are nevertheless classified as real. Panel b keeps the original image, divides it into four tiles, further represents each tile as a grid of local instances, and sends the tile-level and patch-level bags to separate falsification-driven classifiers. A suspicious instance can make the final result fake while spatial information is preserved. Panel c contrasts single-crop inference with multi-patch inference. A single crop receives a score of 0.1 and is classified as real, whereas four local scores of 0.1, 0.1, 0.3, and 0.9 are combined by a maximum operation, allowing the high-scoring region to classify the image as fake.
figures.headline: Single-crop scoring labels a baseball photo real at 0.1, while the maximum over four local scores of 0.1, 0.1, 0.3, and 0.9 labels it fake.
citing_sentences: As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), this paradigm is poorly suited for detecting localized artifacts.
As illustrated in Fig. 1(b), LTF avoids resizing the image or using a single crop.
As shown in Fig. 1(c), FATAS first divides the input image into multiple tiles and predicts a fake score for each tile using an existing detector.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Overview of the proposed hierarchical falsification-driven detection framework. The input image is encoded into two levels of instances by a frozen CLIP-ViT. Cross-Shuffle enhances instance discrimination across bags, and the MIL head aggregates sparse local evidence at each level via gated attention pooling. The final prediction is obtained by fusing the two levels with multi-level supervision.A three-part architecture diagram details the Learning to Falsify framework. In panel a, a frozen CLIP-ViT encodes a tiled input image into patch-level tokens and tile-level CLS tokens. Each level passes through its own Cross-Shuffle module, Transformer block, MIL head, and aggregator. Patch-level and tile-level representations feed their respective classifiers and are also combined by a learned fusion classifier. The three outputs are supervised by patch, tile, and fusion losses. Panel b illustrates Cross-Shuffle: instances from real and fake input bags are collected into separate real and fake pools, then sampled to form recomposed bags. A recomposed real bag contains only real instances, while a recomposed fake bag may mix real and fake instances but retains at least one fake instance. Panel c expands the gated-attention MIL head. Each input instance follows two branches, linear V followed by tanh and linear U followed by sigmoid; their element-wise product is mapped by linear W to attention weights. The weights aggregate instance features into a bag embedding and aggregate instance-classifier outputs into bag logits.
figures.headline: Frozen CLIP-ViT tokens feed tile- and patch-level branches, each with Cross-Shuffle and attention pooling, fused into one prediction.
citing_sentences: As shown in Fig. 2, we propose Learning to Falsify (LTF), a hierarchical detection framework designed to preserve full spatial coverage and identify localized artifacts that can falsify an image’s authenticity.
In the example shown in Fig. 2, $N=4$, the image is represented as one tile-level bag and four patch-level bags.
To overcome this, we propose Cross-Shuffle, which dynamically recomposes bags across images during training, as illustrated in Fig. 2(b).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Performance on high-resolution Chameleon benchmark, where all models are trained on SD v1.4 of GenImage.A horizontal bar chart ranks ten detectors by accuracy on Chameleon. The proposed method, shown in red, ranks first at 72.94 percent. The nine gray baseline bars are PPL at 63.94, AIDE at 62.60, CNNSpot at 60.11, DIRE at 59.71, NPR at 58.13, Fusing at 57.07, FreDetect at 56.86, PatchCraft at 56.32, and UnivFD at 55.62 percent. The proposed method leads the strongest baseline, PPL, by 9.00 percentage points.
figures.headline: LTF scores 72.94 on Chameleon, 9.00 percentage points above the strongest baseline, PPL.
citing_sentences: As shown in Fig. 3, LTF achieves an accuracy of 72.94%, outperforming the second-best method by a substantial margin.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Performance of FATAS across inference settings. “Base” denotes the vanilla detector.Two line charts plot accuracy against the number K of selected patches for NPR, AIDE, CNNSpot, DIRE, and Effort, with Base denoting each detector's original prediction. On Chameleon, AIDE and Effort improve most as K increases: AIDE rises from about 64 percent at Base to about 74 percent at K equals 5, and Effort rises from about 53 to about 73 percent. NPR, CNNSpot, and DIRE remain near 56 to 59 percent with smaller changes. On Midjourney, every detector is above its Base result for K of at least 2. NPR, AIDE, and Effort converge to the mid-to-high 90 percent range by K equals 5. CNNSpot jumps from about 51 percent at Base to about 74 percent at K equals 1 and then gradually declines to about 64 percent at K equals 5, still above Base. DIRE increases from about 45 percent at Base to the low 50 percent range. Most curves flatten after approximately three patches.
figures.headline: FATAS raises AIDE and Effort on Chameleon, and every detector exceeds its base accuracy on Midjourney for K of at least 2.
citing_sentences: Fig. 4 shows that FATAS improves the majority of the evaluated detectors over their base results on both datasets.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Robustness comparison under JPEG compression, Gaussian blur, and image rescaling. Our method achieves more stable performance overall.Three line charts compare the accuracy of the proposed method, UnivFD, and DRCT under image degradation. In the JPEG chart, quality decreases from 100 to 60; the proposed method stays near 96 to 99 percent, while both baselines fall to roughly 84 percent at quality 60. In the Gaussian-blur chart, blur sigma increases from 0.5 to 2.5. All methods begin near 95 to 97 percent, but the proposed method remains around 83 to 88 percent after sigma 1.0, while UnivFD decreases to about 76 percent and DRCT to about 68 percent at sigma 2.5. In the rescaling chart, scale factors range from 0.6 to 1.4. The proposed method is weaker than UnivFD under downscaling at 0.6 and 0.8, peaks near 99 percent at the original scale of 1.0, and stays in the mid-90 percent range for enlargement. DRCT drops sharply at the largest scale, while UnivFD varies more moderately.
figures.headline: The proposed method stays near 96 to 99 percent under JPEG compression, while both baselines fall to roughly 84 percent at quality 60.
citing_sentences: As shown in Fig. 5, our method demonstrates stronger robustness than UnivFD and DRCT across these degradation settings.

abstract: Recent advances in generative models have made synthetic images increasingly photorealistic, posing growing challenges to reliable and generalizable detection of AI-generated images. Existing methods typically rely on holistic image-level classification, which may overlook local artifacts, especially in high-resolution images. To address this limitation, we formulate this task as a falsification-driven multiple instance learning problem, where a single fake patch can falsify the whole image, while a real image requires all patches to be authentic. Based on this formulation, we propose Learning to Falsify (LTF), a hierarchical multiple instance learning framework that models an image as multiple bags of instances across different spatial levels and aggregates their predictions under the falsification-inspired principle. We further introduce Cross-Shuffle during training to encourage the model to learn local artifact evidence rather than image-level shortcuts. Furthermore, we propose the Falsification-driven Test-time Aggregation Strategy (FATAS), a plug-and-play module that extends the same falsification-inspired principle to existing detectors by aggregating patch-level predictions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LTF achieves strong generalization and robustness across multiple benchmarks, while FATAS substantially improves representative detectors in high-resolution scenarios without retraining. Code is available at https://github.com/HuiGuanLab/LTF.git

sections.body: The introduction argues that image-level classifiers, which resize images or use a single crop, lose fine-grained artifacts and give only partial spatial coverage on high-resolution inputs. It proposes a falsification-inspired principle: one fake region rejects an image, while a real image requires all regions to be authentic. The proposed method, Learning to Falsify (LTF), keeps original resolution, builds tile-level and patch-level bags, and adds Cross-Shuffle to reduce image-level shortcuts. FATAS is a training-free test-time method that aggregates tile scores from existing detectors. The section reports gains of over 20 percentage points for CNNSpot on Midjourney and nearly 10 percentage points for AIDE on Chameleon.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Holistic detectors that resize or crop images can miss local artifacts, especially in high-resolution images.

sections.body: The section groups AI-generated image detectors into low-level artifact methods, such as CNNSpot, LGrad, DIRE, and NPR, and high-level semantic methods built on pretrained representations, such as UnivFD, FatFormer, C2P-CLIP, and DRCT. It argues that both families derive image-level predictions from globally aggregated evidence, which makes localized cues hard to capture. It then reviews high-resolution approaches in three groups: whole-image resizing, single-crop analysis, and multi-patch processing with feature aggregation. The authors state that these strategies mainly emphasize broader image coverage. The section is a literature review and reports no experiments.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior detectors resize, crop, or aggregate patches, and local discriminative evidence remains insufficiently modeled.

sections.body: The method keeps each image at original resolution and divides it into N non-overlapping tiles of size 224×224, each encoded by a frozen CLIP-ViT backbone. The CLS token of each tile forms one tile-level bag, and the patch tokens within each tile form a patch-level bag. Cross-Shuffle, active only during training, replaces a fraction of instances in each bag, so every recomposed fake bag keeps at least one fake instance. A gated-attention multiple instance learning head weights instances and sums their logits. A learned gate fuses tile-level and patch-level representations. FATAS, applied at test time, averages the top-k tile probabilities from an existing detector.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Learning to Falsify pools tile and patch instances with gated attention, and Cross-Shuffle recombines bags to block image-level shortcuts.

sections.body: Experiments use a frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 backbone trained for 20 epochs on four A100 GPUs, evaluated on GenImage, DRCT, Chameleon, and HiRes-50K with accuracy and average precision. LTF reports 97.3% on the GenImage Midjourney subset and a mean accuracy of 98.62% on DRCT. On HiRes-50K it averages 81.43% and ranks first across all resolution ranges. In the GenImage ablation, Cross-Shuffle alone raises mAcc from 91.86 to 96.41, and the full model reaches 98.40. FATAS is tested on five detectors on Chameleon and Midjourney, with the largest gains on Midjourney.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: LTF reaches 81.43 average accuracy on HiRes-50K and 72.94 on Chameleon, and FATAS improves several detectors without retraining.

sections.body: The conclusion restates Learning to Falsify as a general principle and summarizes LTF and FATAS. It credits Cross-Shuffle with enabling the multiple instance learning head to capture localized artifacts. The section cites strong cross-dataset generalization on GenImage, DRCT, Chameleon, and HiRes-50K. The stated limitation is computational cost: the approach remains more demanding than single-patch methods, and the authors name efficiency as an important direction for future research. They also suggest extending the principle to AI-generated video detection, without experiments in this section.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: LTF generalizes across four benchmarks but costs more computation than single-patch detectors, which the authors leave as future work.
